## Introduction and overview {#intro}

  ----------------------- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  Code                    Not published — the module is announced in period 1 by the master's brochure; the 2026-2027 SynapseS course description has not been published (the S3/S4 tracks of the catalog are currently empty).

**Audience**: a generative-AI engineer who already knows how to generate and now has to *steer* the output (format, safety, provenance). **Empirical first**: each chapter starts from a concrete failure — a broken JSON despite the prompt, a watermark that no longer shows after a paraphrase — and only then names the technique that fixes it (constrained decoding, steering, RLHF/DPO, watermarking).

The module is organized around four families of control, which together turn a generator that merely produces plausible outputs into a reliable tool.

### What you will be able to do

-   Argue for the need for control (output safety, fidelity to an instruction, intellectual property) and choose the right family of response;
-   Place any technique in the four-family taxonomy (conditioning, guidance, hard constraints, post-processing);
-   Implement grammar- or automaton-constrained decoding, with the masking algorithm detailed step by step;
-   Install and use steering vectors to orient a generation in activation space;
-   Describe RLHF as a control in behavior space, from the reward model to policy optimization;
-   Verify the presence of a textual watermark with the z-test, and discuss its limits;
-   Steer a diffusion via classifier-free guidance, ControlNet, or inversion;
-   Transpose control to graph generators, and measure the fidelity/diversity trade-off — including under attack.

### Where this course fits in the program

M2 module announced for period 1 (slot to be confirmed), on the site's Graph × LLM route: it synthesizes building blocks seen elsewhere in the master rather than introducing a new heavy formalism. **Prerequisites**: diffusion models (DDPM) from [Multimodal Generative AI](../m1p2-multimodal-genai/index.html) ch. 3–4, or, on paths without Multimodal, from [Deep Learning](../m1p1-deep-learning/index.html#ch9) ch. 9 or [Deep Learning P2](../m1p2-deep-learning-p2/index.html#dl-generative) §7.3 — ch. 7 opens with a one-page DDPM recap; the decoding then RLHF from [Large Language Models](../m2-large-language-models/index.html) (revisited in ch. 0 then deepened in ch. 5); graph generation from [Graph ML](../m1p2-graph-ml/index.html#ch9) ch. 9.

**Downstream modules**: the textual watermarking of ch. 6 is taken up and extended on the attestation and anonymization side by [Explainability, Security, Privacy of LLMs](../m2-explainability-security-privacy-llms/index.html) (ch. 9), which also covers safety-side attacks; [Speech Technology for Conversational AI](../m2-speech-technology/index.html) mobilizes the same control reflexes in continuous settings (expressivity, latency, guardrails) in the voice conversational loop.

### Course outline

-   **Reminders: generating, conditioning, decoding** — refreshes sampling, conditioning, and decoding from the prerequisite modules.
-   **Why control: safety, fidelity, intellectual property** — the three industrial and legal motivations that make control unavoidable.
-   **Taxonomy: four families of control** — the reading grid that structures the rest of the course.
-   **Constrained decoding: grammars, automata, masks** — guaranteeing syntactically valid outputs at decoding time, mask by mask.
-   **Steering: controlling in activation space** — orienting the model *during* the forward pass, without retraining.
-   **RLHF: control in behavior space** — what preference alignment can and cannot impose.
-   **Watermarking: proving the origin of a text** — statistically marking a generation and proving it with a z-test.
-   **Controlling diffusions: CFG, ControlNet, inversion** — from classifier-free guidance to editing by inversion.
-   **Controlling graph generators** — imposing constraints and properties where the generated object is discrete and combinatorial.
-   **Evaluating control: fidelity versus diversity** — measuring what every constraint costs the generated distribution.
-   **Attacks on control and robustness** — circumventing grammars, steering, and watermarks, and defending these mechanisms.
-   **Exercises / Labs** — guided implementations: masking automaton, minimal steering, watermark and its test.
-   **References** — the founding papers of each family of control.

### Session plan {#sessions}

**24 h in class (assumed) = 8 sessions of 3 h.** The fiche publishes no teaching hours: 24 h is the M2 volume published for the Large Language Models course (CSC_53432_EP: 24 h, 2 ECTS) and is assumed here; the session split below is our proposal for covering these notes in that time. Level 1 = foundations (reviews, definitions, first worked examples), 2 = core methods, 3 = advanced material (the derivations of the test power and of guidance, entropy bounds, attacks, impossibility results); the level never goes down from one session to the next.

|---|---|---|---|---|

| 3 | 3 h | 2 | ch. 3.2 The masking algorithm, BPE subtleties, grammars | Ex. 1(b)–(e) |
| 4 | 3 h | 2 | ch. 4 Steering vectors; ch. 5 RLHF and DPO as exponential guidance | Ex. 3 |
| 5 | 3 h | 3 | ch. 6 Watermarking: the z-test, its power and the sample size | Ex. 2 |
| 6 | 3 h | 3 | ch. 7 Controlling diffusions: DDPM recap, CFG proof, ControlNet, inversion | Ex. 5 |

**Self-study, outside the 24 h**: no chapter — every chapter is covered in class; the labs (Ex. 1–3 and 6) each need about 2 h of personal work after the session that introduces them.

### How to study this module

-   Learn the taxonomy of ch. 2 by heart and practice classifying every "controlled generative AI" paper or product you come across: it is the module's durable analysis tool.
-   For constrained decoding, simulate the masking algorithm by hand on a mini-automaton: the difficulty is in the implementation, not the idea.
-   Do the labs in order: steering, watermark, and diffusion are better understood once the decoding foundation is mastered.
-   For each technique, note a "cost" line (compute, quality, diversity) and a "guarantee" line: this module is a course in trade-offs.
-   Read ch. 10 last but reread it twice: attacking control is the best way to understand why it holds.

::: note
[The LLGA perspective]{.tag} Control is the exact place where the three pillars of the master — LLMs, multimodal diffusion, graphs — speak the same language: same constraint grammars, same fidelity/diversity trade-off, same attacks. By seeing it first as a cross-cutting problem rather than a collection of per-modality recipes, you will acquire the reflex that distinguishes generative AI engineers and researchers: choosing the level of intervention (data, decoding, activations, behaviors) before choosing the tool.
:::

::: note
[Independent note]{.tag} Place in the two-year path: as in the rest of the master, this module shows the concrete failure modes first and introduces the names and theorems afterwards.
:::

## 0. Reminders: generating, conditioning, decoding {#ch0}

Every control technique of this module modifies one of three things: the way a model generates, the signal it is conditioned on, or the decoding rule that turns its scores into an output. This chapter lists what the prerequisite modules taught about each, so that the later chapters can refer to it.

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Prerequisites (M1 and M2 modules) — what is assumed acquired
:::

-   **Autoregressive generation** (LLMs M2 module, ch. 1-2): factorization
    $$
    p_\theta(y \mid x) = \prod_{t} p_\theta(y_t \mid x, y_{<t}),
    $$
    softmax over the vocabulary (BPE: tokens are *subword units*, not characters), sampling with temperature, top-$k$, top-$p$ (ch. 6 of the same module);
-   **Conditioning and alignment** (LLMs M2 module, ch. 4-5): prompting, SFT, RLHF/DPO/GRPO — we return to these in ch. 5 as *control* mechanisms;
-   **Diffusion** ([Multimodal GenAI](../m1p2-multimodal-genai/index.html#ch3) ch. 3-4; on paths without Multimodal, [Deep Learning](../m1p1-deep-learning/index.html#ch9) ch. 9 or [Deep Learning P2](../m1p2-deep-learning-p2/index.html#dl-generative) §7.3): DDPM, noise prediction $\hat\epsilon_\theta(x_t, t)$, classifier guidance and classifier-*free* guidance (CFG), DDIM — ch. 7 opens with a one-page DDPM recap, proves CFG and introduces inversion, which none of these modules covers;
-   **VAE and ELBO** (Multimodal GenAI ch. 1, or Deep Learning ch. 9 / Deep Learning P2 §7.3): the variational bound, the reconstruction/regularization trade-off;
-   **Graph generation** ([Graph ML](../m1p2-graph-ml/index.html#ch9) M1 module ch. 9): VAE (GraphVAE, NeVAE and its valence masks), autoregressive (GraphRNN), discrete diffusion (DiGress) — ch. 8 recaps the flow GraphAF and takes up their control, as a preview of the Graph Generative Models module (M2, period 2);
-   **Hypothesis testing** ([Refresher Statistics](../m1p1-refresher-statistics/index.html#ch6) M1 module, ch. 6): type I/II error, threshold, $p$-value, central limit theorem — ch. 6 makes intensive use of it.
::::

::: note
[The module's storyline]{.tag} The previous modules answered "how to generate?". This one answers "how to generate *what we want*?". The course's thesis: control is not a patch applied after the fact but a **unified family of mechanisms** — condition, guide, constrain, filter — that recur identically on text (ch. 3-6), images (ch. 7), and graphs (ch. 8), with a common fidelity/diversity trade-off (ch. 9) and a common attack surface (ch. 10).
:::

::: note
[Module status]{.tag} Course offered in the M2 brochure (period 1): the instructors are not yet confirmed. There is therefore no "research of the instructor" chapter; the content follows the standards of the field and the modules already covered by the master (cross-referenced throughout), and will be completed as needed.

## 1. Why control: safety, fidelity, intellectual property {#ch1}

Consider an agent that "follows" its prompt in every respect except the output grammar that the business application expects. This chapter explains why such failures are unavoidable without dedicated mechanisms, and motivates each family of control by the failure it addresses.

::: note
[What breaks]{.tag} Three naive approaches fail in practice: a prompt alone imposes no constraint on the output, rejecting bad outputs and resampling is too costly when good outputs are rare, and a watermark added without care does not survive changes in sampling or editing.
:::

A generator is a *law* over an immense space. Asking it politely (a prompt) only constrains this law statistically: no theorem guarantees the exact format, the safety of the content or the traceability of the origin.

::: def
[Definition 1.1 — Controlling a generator]{.tag} Let $p_\theta(\cdot \mid x)$ be a conditional law over outputs $y \in \mathcal{Y}^*$ (token sequences, images, graphs). **Controlling** means replacing $p_\theta$ with a law $\tilde p$ that

-   **(i)** lives on a specified subset $S \subseteq \mathcal{Y}^*$ (*support constraint*: a language, a JSON schema, a chemical valence); or
-   **(ii)** maximizes in expectation a property $c$ (*fidelity constraint*: following the instruction, the style, the target); or
-   **(iii)** carries a verifiable mark of origin (*provenance constraint*: watermarking).

Chapters 3 to 8 realize (i)-(ii)-(iii) through different mechanisms; ch. 2 will organize them.
:::

::: ex
[Example 1.2 — Three real failures, three needs]{.tag}

1.  **Format safety**: one asks the LLM for a JSON of the form `{"user": ...}`; it replies with a trailing comma, a typographic apostrophe, or worse a preamble "Here is the requested JSON". Any downstream parser breaks. The need: $S =$ *the strict JSON language*, a 100% guarantee — that is ch. 3.
2.  **Fidelity**: one asks for a *neutral* summary in *formal* French; the model slips into casual style one time out of ten. The prompt guarantees nothing; the need is statistical — *soft* steering of the law: ch. 4 and 5.
3.  **Provenance**: a text circulates: human or machine? The classifier is unreliable; the need is *cryptographic*: a statistical mark planted at generation, testable — ch. 6.
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 1.3 — Intellectual property and law as drivers of control]{.tag} Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 ("AI Act", art. 50) imposes **provenance transparency**: providers of generative systems must mark their outputs in a machine-readable way and make them detectable as artificially generated.

Concretely: watermarking (ch. 6) is no longer an academic exercise but a compliance requirement; likewise for audio marking (cf. Signal Processing module) and images. This legal framework motivates the control/robustness articulation (ch. 10): an attackable mark is not a proof.
:::

::: note
[Control cuts across modalities]{.tag} The module's guiding thread: the *same* four mechanisms (condition, guide, constrain the support, filter a posteriori) apply to text, images, and graphs. The tools differ (automata for text; ControlNet and CFG for images; valence masks for graphs), the theory does not. The table in ch. 2 sets the grid; each chapter fills it in for one modality.
:::

## 2. Taxonomy: four families of control {#ch2}

Many techniques claim to "control" a generator; this chapter sorts them into four families according to where they intervene and what they guarantee, so that every later chapter can be placed on the same grid.

::: def
[Definition 2.1 — The four families]{.tag} Let $c$ be the control signal (instruction, target property, admissible language).

1.  **Conditioning**: $c$ enters the model (prompt, prefix, fused embedding); the law becomes $p_\theta(\cdot \mid x, c)$. Zero inference cost, no guarantee — *soft* control;
2.  **Guidance**: one biases the sampling toward $c$ without relearning $p_\theta$ — guided score
    $$
    \hat\epsilon_u + w(\hat\epsilon_c - \hat\epsilon_u)
    $$
    in diffusion (ch. 7), activation steering for LLMs (ch. 4), gradient guidance of flows (ch. 8); the strength $w$ tunes fidelity at the price of diversity;
3.  **Hard constraints**: one restricts the *support* — automaton-constrained decoding (ch. 3), valence masks (ch. 8), inpainting. A 100% guarantee; risk: a *locally* renormalized law, distorted with respect to $p_\theta(\cdot \mid S)$ (theorem 2.2) and possibly impoverished;
4.  **Post-processing / filtering**: generate, check $c$, reject (best-of-$n$, resampling, correction); exact but costly when $c$ is rare.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.2 — The mask guarantees the support, not the conditional law]{.tag} Let $S \subseteq \mathcal{Y}^*$ be a set of admissible outputs and $p_\theta$ an autoregressive law. At step $t$, the mask keeps the set $A_t(y_{<t})$ of the tokens after which the prefix can still be completed into an element of $S$.

Write
$$
Z_t(y_{<t}) = \sum_{v \in A_t(y_{<t})} p_\theta(v \mid x, y_{<t})
$$
for the mass that survives the mask at step $t$. Masked decoding only produces elements of $S$, and it samples them from the **locally renormalized** law

::: key
[Key result — masking renormalizes step by step]{.tag}
$$
\tilde p_\theta(y \mid x) = \prod_{t} \frac{p_\theta(y_t \mid x, y_{<t})}{Z_t(y_{<t})} = \frac{p_\theta(y \mid x)}{\prod_t Z_t(y_{<t})}, \qquad y \in S .
$$
:::

Exact conditioning divides by one constant instead:
$$
p_\theta(y \mid x,\ y \in S) = \frac{p_\theta(y \mid x)}{p_\theta(S \mid x)} .
$$
The two laws coincide if and only if the product of the normalizers $\prod_t Z_t(y_{<t})$ takes the same value for every $y \in S$. In general it does not, and the mask is *not* an exact conditioning.

::: proof
1.  *Support.* Every prefix of an element of $S$ survives the mask, every surviving prefix can still be completed in $S$, and EOS is allowed only on an element of $S$: the masked law lives on $S$.
2.  *Formula.* At step $t$ the decoder draws $y_t$ with probability $p_\theta(y_t \mid x, y_{<t}) / Z_t(y_{<t})$; by the chain rule, the product of the numerators is $p_\theta(y \mid x)$.
3.  *Comparison.* If the product of the normalizers equals a constant $c$ on $S$, summing the masked law over $S$ gives
    $$
    1 = p_\theta(S \mid x) / c ,
    $$
    so the constant is $p_\theta(S \mid x)$ and the two laws coincide. Conversely, if the laws coincide, the product equals $p_\theta(S \mid x)$ for every $y \in S$ (the softmax gives every output a positive probability).

The exact sampler would weight each token by its chance of still ending in $S$,
$$
p_\theta(y_t \mid x, y_{<t}, S) = p_\theta(y_t \mid x, y_{<t})\, \frac{p_\theta(S \mid x, y_{\leq t})}{p_\theta(S \mid x, y_{<t})} ;
$$
the mask only knows whether this chance is positive. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Counterexample — two steps suffice]{.tag} Vocabulary $\{a, b\}$, outputs of two tokens, and the model
$$
p_\theta(a) = p_\theta(b) = \tfrac12, \qquad p_\theta(a \mid a) = 0.1, \quad p_\theta(b \mid a) = 0.9, \qquad p_\theta(a \mid b) = p_\theta(b \mid b) = \tfrac12 .
$$
The constraint forbids $ab$:
$$
S = \{aa,\ ba,\ bb\}, \qquad p_\theta(S) = 0.05 + 0.25 + 0.25 = 0.55 .
$$

-   *Masked decoding.* At step 1 both letters can still reach $S$, so nothing is masked. After $a$ only $a$ survives ($Z_2 = 0.1$), and it is renormalized to probability 1. Hence $\tilde p(aa) = 0.5$ and $\tilde p(ba) = \tilde p(bb) = 0.25$.
-   *Exact conditioning.* $p(aa \mid S) = 0.05 / 0.55 \approx 0.091$ and $p(ba \mid S) = p(bb \mid S) \approx 0.455$.

The mask makes $aa$ 5.5 times too likely, the ratio $p_\theta(S) / Z_2 = 0.55 / 0.1$: at step 1 it ignored that $a$ leads to a near dead end.
:::

::: note
[When the mask is nearly exact, and how to be exact]{.tag} Suppose that at every step the mask removes a mass of at most $\varepsilon$, so that $Z_t \geq 1 - \varepsilon$, on outputs of at most $T$ tokens. Then $p_\theta(S \mid x) \geq (1-\varepsilon)^T$ and, for every $y \in S$,
$$
(1-\varepsilon)^{T} \;\leq\; \frac{\tilde p_\theta(y \mid x)}{p_\theta(y \mid x,\ y \in S)} \;\leq\; (1-\varepsilon)^{-T} .
$$
The mask is nearly free in bias when the model rarely tries to leave $S$ ($\varepsilon T \ll 1$, training data already in $S$), and strongly biased when it often walks towards dead ends, as in the counterexample.

Two exact alternatives exist. Rejection sampling (proposition 2.3) draws exactly from $p_\theta(\cdot \mid S)$, at the expected price of $1/p_\theta(S \mid x)$ passes. Importance sampling keeps the masked proposal and corrects it with the weight $\prod_t Z_t(y_{<t})$, which the decoder computes for free.

Sequential Monte Carlo applies this correction during decoding, resampling a population of partial outputs according to their weights (Lew et al., 2023; Loula et al., ICLR 2025); grammar-aligned decoding estimates the missing look-ahead from earlier samples (Park et al., NeurIPS 2024). Graph Generative Models (period 2) meets the same distortion with valence masks (its ch. 3).
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.3 — Rejection costs $1/p_\star(S)$]{.tag} Filtering by rejection (drawing iid until landing in $S$) realizes $p_\theta(\cdot \mid S)$ *exactly*, but the number of draws follows a geometric law of expectation $1/p_\theta(S \mid x)$.

::: proof
Each draw is an independent Bernoulli trial with success probability $q = p_\theta(S \mid x)$; the waiting time for the first success is geometric,
$$
\mathbb{E}[N] = \sum_{k \geq 1} k(1-q)^{k-1}q = 1/q .
$$
For complex unconstrained JSON, $q$ can be $10^{-2}$ (100 draws on average); for a valid molecule without constraint, GraphAF measures 68% (ch. 8); for a sentence satisfying *both* ten rare constraints, $q$ collapses exponentially — hence the practical advantage of the mask, which pays only a single pass — at the price of the distortion of theorem 2.2. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

| Family | Guarantee | Cost | Diversity | Law modifier |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Conditioning (prompt, instruction) | none | zero | preserved | changes $p_\theta$ itself |
| Guidance (CFG, steering, RLHF) | statistical ($\uparrow w$) | 1-2 passes | decreases with $w$ | $p^{1-w} \cdot \mathrm{score}(c)^w$ |
| Hard constraint (automaton, mask) | 100% on $S$ | 1 pass + mask | bounded by $|S|$ | local renormalization ($\neq p(\cdot \mid S)$ in general) |
| Rejection / best-of-$n$ | 100% (if exact test) | $1/p(S)$ passes | conditioned | exact conditioning $p(\cdot \mid S)$ |

::: note
[Hard or soft: how to choose?]{.tag} A favorite exam question. If failure is *catastrophic* (the parser breaks, the molecule is invalid): hard constraint. If failure is *gradual* (tone, style, relevance): guidance, with the strength tuned by the fidelity/diversity curve of ch. 9. In practice one *stacks*: format constraint (hard) + alignment (RLHF) + watermark (provenance) — the three layers of 2026 production systems, which ch. 10 shows fall… together if one is not careful.
:::

## 3. Constrained decoding: grammars, automata, masks {#ch3}

The technical heart of the module for text: guaranteeing that an output *authorized token by token* belongs to a formal language — regular expression, context-free grammar (JSON, SQL), or logical constraint. The founding idea (PICARD, then Outlines and XGrammar): decoding is a walk in an **automaton**, and the LLM is only allowed to follow valid transitions.

### 3.1. From regex to automaton

::: def
[Definition 3.1 — DFA and regular language]{.tag} A deterministic finite automaton is a quintuple $A = (Q, \Sigma, \delta, q_0, F)$: states $Q$, alphabet $\Sigma$, transition $\delta : Q \times \Sigma \to Q$, initial state $q_0$, accepting states $F$.

One extends $\delta$ to words by $\delta^*(q, uv) = \delta^*(\delta^*(q, u), v)$. The recognized language is
$$
L(A) = \{w \in \Sigma^* : \delta^*(q_0, w) \in F\}.
$$

**Construction**: regex $\to$ $\varepsilon$-NFA (Thompson, linear in the pattern size), then determinization by *subset construction* ($2^{|Q|}$ states at worst, rare in practice).

Course example, the ISO date: `\d{4}-(0[1-9]|1[0-2])-(0[1-9]|[12]\d|3[01])` — a nontrivial $F$: "2026-02-31" must be *syntactically* accepted (calendar semantics is not a simple regular language: we return to this).
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 3.2 — Prune before masking: co-accessibility]{.tag} For masking, one replaces $A$ with its *co-accessible* sub-automaton: one removes the states $q$ from which *no* accepting state is reachable (computation: reverse traversal of the transitions from $F$, $\mathcal{O}(|Q| + |\delta|)$). It is this sub-automaton that guarantees that a prefix always remains *extensible* into a complete word: without pruning, the decoder could lock itself in a dead end (no admissible token, including EOS) and generate indefinitely.
:::

### 3.2. The masking algorithm, in detail

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.3 — Constrained decoding by state→tokens index (Willard & Louf, 2023)]{.tag} Let $V$ be the *tokenizer* vocabulary (multi-character tokens!). One precomputes, for each state $q$ of the pruned DFA, the set of admissible tokens
$$
\mathrm{Adm}(q) = \big\{ v \in V \ : \ \delta^*(q, \mathrm{str}(v)) \ \text{is defined and co-accessible} \big\},
$$
with the table $\mathrm{next}(q, v) = \delta^*(q, \mathrm{str}(v))$.

Constrained decoding replaces each distribution with
$$
p^{\mathrm{mask}}_\theta(v \mid y_{<t}) \propto p_\theta(v \mid y_{<t})\, \mathbf{1}\big[v \in \mathrm{Adm}(q_t)\big], \qquad q_{t+1} = \mathrm{next}(q_t, v_t),
$$
and allows EOS only if $q_t \in F$.

Then every output is in $L(A)$: the guarantee is *structural*, by induction over the steps (theorem 2.2).

::: proof
-   **Complexity.** Precomputation: $|Q| \times |V|$ token reads, each $\mathcal{O}(|v|)$ transitions — once and for all (and shareable between requests of the same grammar: XGrammar further accelerates by separating *context-independent* tokens, pre-checked globally, from *dependent* ones, the only ones resimulated).
-   **Online**: one lookup per step, $\mathcal{O}(1)$ — the overhead over the LLM pass ($\mathcal{O}(n^2)$) is negligible.
-   **BPE subtlety**: a token is not a character; `"12"` and `"12/"` are two distinct tokens; the definition of $\mathrm{Adm}$ copes with this because $\delta^*$ reads *the string* of the token, character by character — the DFA does not even know it is being run over BPEs.

Instructive counterexample: a token can cross the boundary of the language (`"},"` is valid at the end of JSON, `"},x"` is not); this is precisely why one must index over *tokens* and not over characters. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

```python
# pedagogical skeleton: automaton-based constrained decoding (cf. lab 1)
import torch

class DfaMask:
    """dfa: transitions[q] = {character: q2}, accepting = {q...} (already pruned)."""

    def __init__(self, dfa, tokenizer):
        self.index = {}                        # q -> {token_id: q2}
        for q in dfa.states:                   # precomputation O(|Q| x |V| x |v|)
            self.index[q] = {}
            for tid, s in tokenizer.vocab.items():
                q2 = dfa.walk(q, s)            # read character by character
                if q2 is not None:             # None = dead prefix
                    self.index[q][tid] = q2

    def mask(self, logits, q):
        mask = torch.full_like(logits, float("-inf"))
        for tid in self.index[q]:
            mask[tid] = 0.0
        return logits + mask                   # -inf = forbidden

# generation loop (the DFA is the state of the control, the LLM provides the logits)
#   q = q0
#   while True:
#       logits = model(y)[..., -1, :]
#       if q in dfa.accepting:  logits[eos_id] = 0.0    # exit allowed
#       v = sample(softmax(mask(logits, q)))
#       if v == eos_id:  break
#       q = index[q][v] ; y = torch.cat([y, v])         # invariant: y in L(A)
```

::: ex
[Example 3.4 — A date by hand]{.tag} Constraint with a month check, `\d{2}/(0[1-9]|1[0-2])/\d{4}`. After `"26/0"`, the state encodes "second digit of the month in progress, 0 already seen"; the token `"0"` is masked (only `1`-`9` complete a month `01`-`09`), and so is `"/"`. Conversely, if the first digit of the month were `1`, the second would be restricted to `0-2`.

Writing the table $\mathrm{Adm}(q)$ for these states is exercise 1; the classic pitfall: allowing the token `"13"` as a single BPE block when the state accepts only `"1"` followed by `"0-2"` — `"13"` must be masked *as a whole*.
:::

::: note
[Beyond regular languages: grammars and JSON Schema]{.tag} Regular languages cannot express nesting (`{"a": {"b": ...}}` of arbitrary depth). One needs context-free grammars: PICARD (Scholak et al., EMNLP 2021) constrains a T5 on SQL by *incremental parsing* (forbidden logits are set to $-\infty$ as soon as the token makes the derivation dead).

XGrammar compiles EBNF/JSON Schema into nearly free online masks (2-10× faster than the previous state of the art). In 2026 industrial practice: *every* LLM tool call (function calling) goes through a grammar mask — the output is valid JSON *by construction*. Cf. LLMs module (M2) ch. 8 for the agent layer.
:::

## 4. Steering: controlling in activation space {#ch4}

Constrained decoding acts on the *outputs*. Steering acts *inside* the network: if concepts ("positivity", "gender", "refusal") are encoded by directions of the activation space, then moving them *should* move the behavior. This is the most fascinating and least guaranteed control of the module.

::: def
[Definition 4.1 — Steering vector (ActAdd, Turner et al. 2023)]{.tag} Let $h^{(l)}(x) \in \mathbb{R}^d$ be the residual activation of layer $l$ after reading the prefix $x$. For two contrasted prompts $x^+$ ("Love") and $x^-$ ("Hate"), one defines
$$
v = h^{(l)}(x^+) - h^{(l)}(x^-) \in \mathbb{R}^d,
$$
and, during generation, one replaces
$$
h^{(l)}(x_t) \leftarrow h^{(l)}(x_t) + \alpha\, v
$$
at *every* step (and often on the first token only); $\alpha \in [-4, 4]$ is the guidance strength.

The model, the weights, the prompt: nothing changes — only a vector is added.
:::

::: ex
[Example 4.2 — The founding experiment, described step by step (to replay in lab 3)]{.tag} Model: GPT-2 (124M-1.5B in the paper; the lab uses the small one).

1.  Compute $v$ = $h^{(6)}(\texttt{Love}) - h^{(6)}(\texttt{Hate})$.
2.  Generate 200 continuations of the prompt "I want to tell you something" *without* steering, then with $\alpha = +1$, then $\alpha = -1$.
3.  Count the marriage-related words ("love, wedding, bride, forever…"): their frequency jumps by a factor of several tens at $\alpha = +1$, drops below the baseline at $\alpha = -1$.
4.  Measure the perplexity on OpenWebText: nearly unchanged at $\alpha = \pm 1$, it explodes toward $|\alpha| \gtrsim 5$ (degenerate outputs).
5.  Observe the inter-layer disagreement: steering works "better" (strong effect, coherent text) on some layers (middle of the network) than others — one more hyperparameter.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.3 — Why a simple addition shifts the output (first-order analysis)]{.tag} Let $W_U$ denote the unembedding matrix (output layer). The logit of token $w$ equals $\ell_w = \langle W_U^{(w)}, h^{(L)} \rangle$ (final layer, ignoring the softmax).

If the steered residual $h^{(L)} + \alpha v^{(L)}$ stays within the network's linearity domain, then
$$
\Delta \ell_w \;=\; \alpha\, \langle W_U^{(w)}, v^{(L)} \rangle\ :
$$
*all tokens aligned with the direction $v$ are favored proportionally to $\alpha$* — a global, monotone reweighting, even before any nonlinear effect.

::: proof
Differentiability: to first order, $h^{(L)} \mapsto \ell_w$ is affine;
$$
\Delta \ell_w = \nabla_h \ell_w^\top (\alpha v) = \alpha \langle W_U^{(w)}, v\rangle.
$$
This is exactly the structure of *guidance* (ch. 2, family 2): each token's logit is shifted by a "compatibility with the direction" score.

The difference from the mask: here no logit is sent to $-\infty$ — the law keeps full support, the control is soft; and the linear approximation becomes false as $\alpha$ grows, hence the observed degeneration. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: note
[The steering family in 2026: reading, writing, weights]{.tag}

-   **Read**: probing and concept directions (cf. Explainability module ch. 1);
-   **write**: ActAdd (difference of two activations), contrastive activation addition (differences averaged over pairs of behaviors), inference-time intervention (moving activations *toward* the truthfulness direction), representation engineering (Zou et al., 2023: extracting via self-interpretation directions of honesty, refusal, bias and subtracting/adding them);
-   **on weights**: task arithmetic (Ilharco et al., ICLR 2023): adding to the *weights* the difference between a fine-tuned model and the base model — the same "add a direction" gesture moved from one space to another, composable (adding two tasks, canceling one by subtraction).

Common limits: empirical choice of layer and $\alpha$, non-monotone effects, fragile out-of-distribution generalization — and no support guarantee: to *truly* forbid a format, only ch. 3 applies.
:::

## 5. RLHF: control in behavior space {#ch5}

RLHF was presented as alignment (cf. LLMs M2 module ch. 5 — we do not redo its practice); here we reread it as a *control* mechanism, and we prove that it is — mathematically — the *twin* of classifier-free guidance in ch. 7. This double reading is the module's synthesis point.

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.1 — RLHF = exponential guidance of the output law (closed-form solution proved)]{.tag} The alignment program with KL penalty reads
$$
\pi^* = \arg\max_{\pi}\ \mathbb{E}_{y \sim \pi(\cdot \mid x)}\big[r(x, y)\big] \;-\; \beta\, \mathrm{KL}\big(\pi(\cdot \mid x)\,\|\,\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot \mid x)\big).
$$
Its unique solution is

::: key
[Key result — closed form of the KL-regularized policy]{.tag}
$$
\pi^*(y \mid x) \;=\; \frac{1}{Z(x)}\, \pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y \mid x)\, \exp\big(r(x, y)/\beta\big), \qquad Z(x) = \sum_{y'} \pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y' \mid x) e^{r(x,y')/\beta}.
$$
:::

::: proof
One maximizes over the law $\pi$ (an infinite-dimensional variable). Set
$$
J(\pi) = \mathbb{E}_\pi[r] - \beta\,\mathbb{E}_\pi[\log \frac{\pi}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}].
$$

First order: for every perturbation $\pi + \varepsilon(\nu - \pi)$ ($\nu$ any law),
$$
\frac{d}{d\varepsilon} J\big|_{\varepsilon=0} = \mathbb{E}_{\nu}[r - \beta\log\frac{\pi}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}} - \beta - c] = 0
$$
for all $\nu$, where $c$ is the multiplier of the constraint $\sum_y \pi(y) = 1$.

This forces
$$
r(x,y) - \beta \log\frac{\pi(y \mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y \mid x)}
$$
to be constant in $y$:
$$
\log \frac{\pi}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}} = r/\beta + \mathrm{const},
$$
giving the result (the constant is fixed by normalization; the strict concavity of the KL gives uniqueness).

**Control reading**: the aligned policy is the reference law *reweighted by an exponential factor in the reward*, exactly as CFG reweights $p(x_t)$ by $p(c \mid x_t)^w$ (ch. 7).

$\beta$ (the inverse of the reward temperature) plays the role of the guidance strength $w$, and the KL is the *budget* of allowed deviation — high fidelity to $r$, low diversity if $\beta$ is small. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: prop
[Proposition 5.2 — DPO: the same solution, without a reward model]{.tag} By rewriting
$$
r = \beta \log \frac{\pi^*}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}} + \beta\log Z,
$$
the preference between $y_w \succ y_l$ is expressed directly in policies: the DPO loss
$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DPO}} = -\log \sigma\Big(\beta \log\tfrac{\pi_\theta(y_w \mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_w \mid x)} - \beta \log\tfrac{\pi_\theta(y_l \mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_l \mid x)}\Big)
$$
is the likelihood of the preferences *under the closed form of theorem 5.1*: DPO learns the same exponential guidance by direct regression on pairs.

GRPO (group-relative reinforcement) is its extension via within-group comparisons — developed in detail in ch. 5 of the LLMs module (M2), which should be consulted for the actual training.
:::

::: note
[Reward hacking: when control misses its target]{.tag} The reward is a *spec*; the model optimizes the spec, not the intention. The mechanism (well documented): the closed-form solution 5.1 concentrates mass on the peaks of $r$ — including *artifactual* peaks (long answers, sycophancy, formats favored by the reward model).

The KL brakes (budget!), without forbidding: with KL budget zero, $\pi^* = \pi_{\mathrm{ref}}$; as $\beta \to 0$, collapse onto the argmax of $r$. Same structure as the CFG fidelity/diversity trade-off — ch. 9 for the measurement, ch. 10 for the attack (exploiting the rewarder's artifacts is a control hijack).
:::

## 6. Watermarking: proving the origin of a text {#ch6}

Provenance constraint (def. 1.1 iii): modify *the generation* so that outputs carry a secret statistical mark, verifiable without wiggle room. The green/red scheme of Kirchenbauer et al. (ICML 2023) is the most taught because its test can be proved at the M2 level — it is also the bridge with the audio watermarking of the Signal Processing module and ch. 9 of the Explainability module.

The law of the test under the null hypothesis is proved in [Large Language Models ch. 9](../m2-large-language-models/index.html#ch9); this chapter recalls it in one step and adds what that course leaves out: the power of the test and the text length it requires.

::: def
[Definition 6.1 — Green/red watermark (Kirchenbauer et al., 2023)]{.tag} **Key**: secret $k$.

**At every step**: one hashes the *previous* token with $k$ (PRF $h_k$), the result serves as a pseudo-random seed to partition the vocabulary: a *green list* $G_k(y_{t-1})$ of fraction $\gamma$ (typically $\gamma = 0.5$), the rest in the red list.

**Generation**: before the softmax, one adds $\delta$ to the green logits (typ. $\delta = 2$):
$$
\ell^{(t)}_v \leftarrow \ell^{(t)}_v + \delta \cdot \mathbf{1}\big[v \in G_k(y_{t-1})\big].
$$

**Detection**: knowing $k$, one recounts the greens.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 6.2 — The z-test and its power (H0: unmarked text)]{.tag} Let a suspect text of $T$ tokens, $s = \sum_{t=1}^T \mathbf{1}[y_t \in G_k(y_{t-1})]$ its number of greens, and the statistic

::: key
[Key result — watermark z-score]{.tag}
$$
z \;=\; \frac{s - \gamma T}{\sqrt{T\, \gamma (1 - \gamma)}}.
$$
:::

Under the null hypothesis "text written without knowledge of $k$" (hence human, or an unmarked model), $z$ converges in law to $\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ as $T \to \infty$, and one rejects $H_0$ at level $\alpha$ if
$$
z > z_{1-\alpha} = \Phi^{-1}(1 - \alpha).
$$

If a marked text draws a green token with probability $p_\delta > \gamma$ at each step, the power of this test and the length needed for a power $1 - \beta$ are approximately
$$
\mathbb{P}(z > z_{1-\alpha} \mid H_1) \approx \Phi\!\left(\frac{(p_\delta - \gamma)\sqrt{T} - z_{1-\alpha}\sqrt{\gamma(1-\gamma)}}{\sqrt{p_\delta(1-p_\delta)}}\right), \qquad T \approx \left(\frac{z_{1-\alpha}\sqrt{\gamma(1-\gamma)} + z_{1-\beta}\sqrt{p_\delta(1-p_\delta)}}{p_\delta - \gamma}\right)^{2}.
$$

::: proof
1.  *Law under H0* (proved in [LLMs Theorem 9.3](../m2-large-language-models/index.html#ch9), recalled here). The pseudo-random seed $h_k(y_{t-1})$ makes each token of an unmarked text green with probability $\gamma$, so $s \sim \mathrm{Bin}(T, \gamma)$ (neglecting the weak sequential dependence). The De Moivre-Laplace theorem gives $z \Rightarrow \mathcal{N}(0,1)$.
2.  *Threshold*. P(false positive) $= \alpha$: with $z_{\mathrm{threshold}} = 4$, $\alpha \approx 3.2 \times 10^{-5}$ — a human text is accused once in \~30,000.
3.  *Law under H1*. For a marked text, each step draws a green with probability $p_\delta > \gamma$ (the bump $\delta$ favors greens). With the same heuristic $s \sim \mathrm{Bin}(T, p_\delta)$, hence
    $$
    \mathbb{E}[z \mid H_1] = \frac{(p_\delta - \gamma)\sqrt{T}}{\sqrt{\gamma(1-\gamma)}}, \qquad \mathrm{Var}(z \mid H_1) = \frac{p_\delta(1-p_\delta)}{\gamma(1-\gamma)} .
    $$
4.  *Power and length*. Approximating $z$ under H1 by a Gaussian with these two moments, the power is the probability that this Gaussian exceeds $z_{1-\alpha}$: this is the first formula. Setting the argument of $\Phi$ equal to $z_{1-\beta}$ and solving for $\sqrt{T}$ gives the second.

With $\gamma = 0.5$, $\delta = 2$, $p_\delta \approx 0.7$-0.8 in practice, and $T = 200$, $\mathbb{E}[z] \approx 5.7$-8.5 — detection is nearly certain. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 6.3 — The test in numbers (exercise 2 in full)]{.tag} $T = 200$, $\gamma = 0.5$. A marked text observes $s = 150$ (75% greens):
$$
z = (150 - 100)/\sqrt{200 \times 0.25} = 50/\sqrt{50} \approx 7.07
$$
— massive rejection of H0.

A *typical* human text would have $s \in [87, 113]$ at 95% ($z \in [-1.96, 1.96]$).

Bonus question: how many tokens are needed to distinguish $\gamma = 0.5$ from $p_\delta = 0.6$ at level 5% (two-sided, as above) with power 0.9? The length formula of theorem 6.2, with the two-sided quantile $\Phi^{-1}(0.975)$ in place of $z_{1-\alpha}$, gives
$$
T \approx \big(\Phi^{-1}(0.975)\sqrt{0.5 \times 0.5} + \Phi^{-1}(0.9)\sqrt{0.6 \times 0.4}\big)^2 / (0.6 - 0.5)^2 = (0.98 + 0.63)^2 / 0.01 \approx 260.
$$

The required length scales as $(p_\delta - \gamma)^{-2}$: halving the bias toward green tokens multiplies by four the length of text needed to detect it — this is *the* scaling law of watermarking.
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 6.4 — The family: distortion, robustness, undetectability]{.tag} Four descendants structure the field.

1.  **Unigram** (Zhao et al., 2023): the green list is *fixed* (context-independent) — robust to paraphrase (tokens survive reordering), at the price of lower detectability at given $T$.
2.  **Gumbel/Aaronson**: the token draw follows an inverse rank sampled by PRF — *distortion-free* (the per-step marginal law is exactly the model's); the score becomes a sum of logs.
3.  **Kuditipudi et al. (2023)**: marking by a re-parameterizable *key sequence*, zero distortion and robust to edits;
4.  **SynthID-Text** (Dathathri et al., Nature 2024): deployed in production at Gemini's scale — a *tournament* of keys per step, qualitatively preserved, corpus-aggregated test.

In contrast: the negative result of Sadasivan et al. (2023) — against a paraphraser *good enough*, every detector (watermark included) tends toward blindness.

Christ, Gunn & Zamir (2024) show the other extreme: a cryptographic watermark can be made *undetectable* without the key (marked outputs are computationally indistinguishable from the model's), but such constructions are fragile to edits. Ch. 10 returns to this in attack mode.
:::

::: note
[Tuning: $\gamma$, $\delta$, and the triple trade-off]{.tag} Increasing $\delta$ → easy detection ($p_\delta \to 1$) but degraded text (the choice is biased toward greens even when a red was the "right" word); decreasing $\gamma$ → rare green lists, a sharper signal but a stiffer constraint on quality.

In production one targets $\gamma = 0.25$-0.5, $\delta = 1$-2: imperceptible quality loss (evaluated by perplexity and human tests), $z > 4$ reached from $T \approx 50$-100. The same bipolar tuning *signal quality / law fidelity* structures *audio* watermarking (WavMark, AudioSeal — cf. Speech Technology module ch. 9): two modalities, one theory.
:::

## 7. Controlling diffusions: CFG, ControlNet, inversion {#ch7}

Control of diffusion models was introduced in M1 (Multimodal GenAI module ch. 4); here we give the short *proof* of classifier-free guidance, then the two industrial standards of spatial control (ControlNet) and editing (inversion, which no M1 module covers). The box below recalls the DDPM notation for students who met diffusion in a Deep Learning course rather than in Multimodal GenAI.

::: recap
[Recap — DDPM in one page]{.tag} *Forward process.* A fixed chain adds Gaussian noise in $T$ steps, with a variance schedule $\beta_t$ and $\bar\alpha_t = \prod_{s \leq t}(1 - \beta_s)$. Its marginal is explicit, so a noisy sample is drawn in one shot:
$$
x_t = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\, x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_t}\, \epsilon, \qquad \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I).
$$
With $T \approx 1000$ steps and $\bar\alpha_T \approx 0$, the last state is almost pure Gaussian noise.

*Training.* A network $\hat\epsilon_\theta(x_t, t)$ predicts the noise that was added, for a step $t$ drawn uniformly; the simplified variational bound of Ho et al. is a regression
$$
\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{x_0, t, \epsilon}\, \big\| \epsilon - \hat\epsilon_\theta\big(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\, x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_t}\, \epsilon,\ t\big) \big\|^2 .
$$
The optimal predictor is the posterior mean of the noise, which is proportional to the score,
$$
\hat\epsilon(x_t, t) = -\sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_t}\, \nabla_{x_t} \log p(x_t),
$$
the parametrization used in theorem 7.1.

*Sampling.* Start from $x_T \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$ and denoise step by step, with $\alpha_t = 1 - \beta_t$ and $z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$:
$$
x_{t-1} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}\Big(x_t - \frac{\beta_t}{\sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_t}}\, \hat\epsilon_\theta(x_t, t)\Big) + \sigma_t z ,
$$
with, for instance, $\sigma_t^2 = \beta_t$; each of the $T$ steps costs one network evaluation.

*DDIM* reuses the same trained network with a deterministic step: it predicts the clean image, then re-noises it to the level $t-1$,
$$
\hat x_0 = \frac{x_t - \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_t}\, \hat\epsilon_\theta(x_t, t)}{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}}, \qquad x_{t-1} = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}\, \hat x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_{t-1}}\, \hat\epsilon_\theta(x_t, t).
$$
It runs on a subsequence of 20 to 50 steps, and the same initial noise always gives the same image: inversion (proposition 7.3) exploits exactly this determinism.

*Conditioning.* The network also takes a condition $c$, replaced by a null token during part of the training: one network then gives both $\hat\epsilon_c$ and $\hat\epsilon_u$, the two ingredients of classifier-free guidance. Full treatment: [Multimodal GenAI](../m1p2-multimodal-genai/index.html#ch3) ch. 3–4, [Deep Learning P2](../m1p2-deep-learning-p2/index.html#dl-generative) Definition 7.10, [Deep Learning](../m1p1-deep-learning/index.html#diffusion) section 9.4.
:::

### 7.1. CFG: the short proof

:::: thm
[Theorem 7.1 — Classifier guidance and CFG are the same exponential reweighting]{.tag} Let $\hat\epsilon_c, \hat\epsilon_u$ denote the noises predicted with/without conditioning, and
$$
\hat\epsilon_w = \hat\epsilon_u + w\,(\hat\epsilon_c - \hat\epsilon_u)
$$
the CFG prediction. Since
$$
\hat\epsilon(x_t, t) = -\sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_t}\, \nabla_{x_t} \log p(x_t)
$$
(score parametrization), the CFG combination realizes
$$
\nabla_{x_t} \log p_w(x_t) \;=\; \nabla_{x_t} \log p(x_t) + w\, \nabla_{x_t} \log p(c \mid x_t) \;=\; \nabla_{x_t} \log \big[p(x_t \mid c)^w \, p(x_t)^{1-w}\big],
$$
that is, sampling from the *reweighted* law

::: key
[Key result — CFG samples a reweighted law]{.tag}
$$
p_w \propto p(x_t \mid c)^w p(x_t)^{1-w}
$$
:::

— exactly the family of theorem 5.1 (RLHF) with $w \leftrightarrow 1/\beta$.

::: proof
Linearity of the score: $\hat\epsilon_w = (1 - w)\hat\epsilon_u + w \hat\epsilon_c$ (rewrite the combination); each term is proportional to the gradient of the corresponding log-density, so the sum is the gradient of the *sum* of the logs.

For the conditional term, Bayes' rule $p(x_t \mid c) \propto p(c \mid x_t)\, p(x_t)$ gives
$$
\nabla \log p(x_t \mid c)^w p(x_t)^{1-w} = w\nabla\log p(c \mid x_t) + \nabla \log p(x_t)
$$
— which is precisely the formula of *classifier guidance* with weight $w$: CFG obtains it *without a classifier*, by training the same network with conditioning dropout.

-   At $w = 1$: pure conditional model;
-   $w > 1$: over-guidance (fidelity $\uparrow$, diversity $\downarrow$, color saturation — the classic visual symptom);
-   $w < 1$: interpolation toward the unconditional. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

### 7.2. ControlNet: spatial control, without breaking the pre-training

:::: thm
[Theorem 7.2 — ControlNet architecture (Zhang, Rao & Agrawala, ICCV 2023)]{.tag} Let $F(x ; \Theta)$ be a frozen UNet block (operation on the activation $x$ of layer $i$). ControlNet branches off a *trainable copy* initialized at $\Theta$ and locks the output with two *null* convolutions (zero-convolutions):
$$
y \;=\; F(x;\Theta) \;+\; Z_2\Big(F_c\big(Z_1(c;\Theta_{z_1});\ \Theta_c\big);\ \Theta_{z_2}\Big),
$$
where $c$ is the control map (Canny edges, depth, skeletal pose…); $Z_i$ is a $1\times1$ convolution with *zero weights at initialization*.

::: proof
-   **Identity property at the start.** At $t = 0$: $Z_2(\cdot) = W_2 \, h = 0$ since $W_2 = 0$ — the branch outputs exactly zero, and the composed model is *identically* the pre-trained model: fine-tuning starts from the initial quality, without "catastrophic shift".
-   **The gradient does not vanish.** The derivative of the output with respect to $W_2$ equals $\partial y / \partial W_2 = h_c \neq 0$ (the copy $F_c$, initialized at $\Theta$, produces nonzero activations).

    The first update pulls $W_2$ away from zero, which then *unlocks* the gradients toward $F_c$ and $Z_1$ (which were zero as long as $W_2 = 0$, by the chain rule).

Compare the naive alternative (branching $F_c$ directly): at step 0, uncontrolled random noise is added to the activations of the frozen UNet and destroys the coherence of the output for hundreds of steps. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: note
[Why a "copy" and not a "new network"]{.tag} The copy inherits the pre-trained features: control learns *the correspondence control map → existing rich features*, not vision from scratch — hence the data efficiency (a few thousand pairs suffice for a new type of control). This is a general pattern of the module: condition around a frozen model and protect the interface with an identity initialization (the mask of ch. 3 is the exact analogue for discrete slots: allow only what preserves the invariant).
:::

### 7.3. Editing a real image: inversion and null-text

::: prop
[Proposition 7.3 — DDIM inversion and its failure under CFG]{.tag} DDIM defines a deterministic step linking $x_t$ and $x_{t-1}$ via the prediction $\hat x_0(x_t, c)$ (recap box above; Multimodal GenAI Construction 4.2). *Inversion*, new in this module, traverses the relation backwards to recover the noise that generates a given real image, approximating the noise prediction at $x_{t+1}$ by the one at $x_t$:
$$
x_{t+1} = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t+1}}\, \hat x_0(x_t, c) + \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_{t+1}}\; \hat\epsilon_c(x_t, c).
$$

With CFG, the applied "noise" depends on a $w$-combination of the conditional/unconditional predictions; inversion becomes an implicit equation (the step depends on $x_t$ through two networks): error accumulates, the reconstruction drifts.

**Null-text inversion** (Mokady et al., CVPR 2023): keep the inversion trajectory as an *anchor* and optimize, step by step, the *null* condition embedding $c_\varnothing^{(t)}$ to minimize
$$
\|\hat x_0\big(x_t; c, c_\varnothing^{(t)}\big) - x_0\|^2
$$
— a few dozen gradient steps per image.

Editing (Prompt-to-Prompt: substituting the cross-attention maps; InstructPix2Pix: learning editing on synthetic data) then operates *along* this faithful trajectory.
:::

::: ex
[Example 7.4 — CFG by hand (pen-and-paper)]{.tag} Vocabulary of 3 artistic "directions", logits of step $t$ without conditioning:
$$
(\text{painting}: 2.0,\ \text{photo}: 1.5,\ \text{3D}: 0.5);
$$
with condition "watercolor": $(3.0,\ 0.5,\ 0.5)$.

-   Without guidance the softmax of $u$ is $\approx (0.55,\ 0.33,\ 0.12)$.
-   At $w = 3$: guided logits
    $$
    u + w(c - u) = (1-w)\,u + w\,c = (5.0,\ -1.5,\ 0.5)
    $$
    — softmax $\approx (0.988,\ 0.001,\ 0.011)$.

The target style crushes the distribution. $w = 8$ → a single mode survives: the curve of ch. 9, readable on a single step.
:::

## 8. Controlling graph generators {#ch8}

Synthesis chapter, previewed here and developed in the Graph Generative Models module (M2, period 2). We start from the graph generators of [Graph ML ch. 9](../m1p2-graph-ml/index.html#ch9) (NeVAE and its valence masks, GraphRNN, DiGress), add the flow GraphAF in the box below, and place the three controls on the grid of ch. 2: the theory of control is the *same* as for text and images.

::: recap
[Recap — GraphAF, a flow that generates a molecule step by step]{.tag} GraphAF (Shi et al., ICLR 2020) keeps the sequential order of GraphRNN (Graph ML 9.4): at each step it adds an atom, then its bonds to the atoms already placed. Each decision is a one-hot vector $x$ (atom type or bond type), made continuous by *dequantization*, $\tilde x = x + u$ with $u$ uniform on $[0,1)^d$.

The continuous decision comes from a Gaussian latent through an affine map whose shift and scale are computed by a graph neural network (Graph ML ch. 5) on the partial graph $G_{<t}$:
$$
\tilde x_t = \mu_t(G_{<t}) + \sigma_t(G_{<t}) \odot z_t, \qquad z_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I).
$$
The change of variables ([Refresher Statistics](../m1p1-refresher-statistics/index.html#ch2) Theorem 2.4) gives the exact log-likelihood, maximized during training:
$$
\log p(\tilde x_t \mid G_{<t}) = \log \mathcal{N}(z_t;\, 0, I) - \sum_k \log \sigma_{t,k}(G_{<t}) .
$$
At sampling time, the argmax of $\tilde x_t$ gives the discrete choice, and a valence check rejects and redraws a bond that would exceed the valence of an atom. Graph Generative Models ch. 4 develops flows in full.
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 8.1 — Three controls, three mechanisms, one grid]{.tag}

1.  **Hard constraints: chemical valence**. Each decoding step masks the bonds that would exceed the remaining valence $r_v$ of atom $v$.

    NeVAE (AAAI 2019) pushes validity above 90% without post-processing (versus a few percent otherwise); GraphAF masks likewise and reaches 100% with rules (68% without).

    This is theorem 2.2 on graphs: validity is guaranteed by construction, and the masked law is the locally renormalized one — with the same distortion with respect to exact conditioning on the legal set $\mathcal{L}$;
2.  **Guidance toward a property**: to favor a property $Q(G)$ (solubility, docking), the GraphAF paper fine-tunes the pretrained flow by reinforcement learning with reward $Q$ — the KL-regularized exponential reweighting of theorem 5.1. Because each decision is an invertible map of a Gaussian $z_t$, one can also move $z_t$ along $\nabla_{z_t} Q(G_t)$ *during* generation (latent gradient guidance, as in the one-shot flow MoFlow, 2020): the step size plays the role of the guidance strength, and the fidelity/diversity trade-off of ch. 9 is measured on it;
3.  **Conditioning + inpainting**: DiGress (ICLR 2023) trains the denoiser with a descriptor $c$ sometimes masked (classifier-free: thm 7.1 transposed) and freezes partial scaffolds; the discrete posterior allows generating *around* an imposed motif — the exact analogue of the image null-text/inpainting of ch. 7.
:::

  Control               Mechanism (ch. 2)                Graph ML (M1) → GGM (P2)     Text analogue        Image analogue
  --------------------- -------------------------------- ---------------------------- -------------------- --------------------
  Chemical validity     mask (local renormalization)     9.3 → ch. 3 (NeVAE)          automaton of ch. 3   —
  Target property $Q$   RL fine-tuning or guidance       box above → ch. 4 (GraphAF)  steering (ch. 4)     CFG (ch. 7)
  Imposed scaffold      conditioning + inpainting        9.5 → ch. 5 (DiGress)        forced prefix        null-text (ch. 7)
  Text → graph          heavy conditioning (LLM)         ch. 10 → ch. 7               prompting            full text-to-image

::: note
[What graphs teach control]{.tag} Two specific lessons.

1.  *Local* constraints (valence) are trivially masked, *global* constraints (connectivity, ring size) are not: the corresponding automaton would be exponential — the search for "tractable global constraints" is open;
2.  the evaluation of control is the most mature there (validity/uniqueness/novelty + FCD; Graph ML 9.6, developed in Graph Generative Models ch. 6) — it is the template of ch. 9.
:::

## 9. Evaluating control: fidelity versus diversity {#ch9}

Controlling without measuring is believing. This chapter sets the protocol: two axes (fidelity, diversity), one curve (the strength sweep), one decomposition (precision/recall), and a bound showing that the trade-off is *structural*, not an engineering defect.

::: def
[Definition 9.1 — Fidelity and diversity]{.tag} **Control fidelity**:
$$
\mathrm{Fid}(S) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i \mathbf{1}[y_i \in S]
$$
(pass rate; or a continuous metric — property score, similarity to the prompt).

**Diversity**: mean intra-batch distance
$$
\mathrm{Div} = \frac{2}{n(n-1)}\sum_{i<j} d(y_i, y_j)
$$
(self-BLEU for text, LPIPS distance for images, Tanimoto distance between fingerprints for molecules — Graph Generative Models ch. 6, period 2); or entropy of the effective law.

**Quality** in the data-fidelity sense: FID (recall of the Multimodal GenAI module ch. 7), perplexity under a reference model.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 9.2 — The trade-off is structural (entropy bound)]{.tag} Let $S \subset \mathcal{Y}^*$ be the admissible set ($|S| = m$ finite; for sequences, consider outputs of length $\leq L$ over a vocabulary of size $k$: $m \leq k^L$, the whole space).

Every law $\tilde p$ supported on $S$ satisfies

::: key
[Key result — entropy ceiling of a constrained law]{.tag}
$$
H(\tilde p) \;\leq\; \log m \;=\; H_{\max}(\mathcal{Y}^{\leq L}) \;-\; \log\frac{k^L}{m}.
$$
:::

::: proof
Entropy is maximal for the uniform law (Gibbs' inequality: for every $p$ on $S$,
$$
\mathrm{KL}(p \,\|\, \mathrm{Unif}_S) = \log m - H(p) \geq 0,
$$
with equality iff uniform).

Support constraint → entropy ceiling lowered by $\log(k^L/m)$: each division of the number of admissible outputs by $e$ costs 1 nat of maximal diversity.

Guidance acts likewise but *smoothly*: $p_w \propto p^{1-w}\mathrm{score}(c)^w$ concentrates mass on the modes compatible with $c$ — the effective entropy decreases monotonically in the usual cases (theorems 5.1 and 7.1: the KL from the start is exactly the price paid); hence the curve. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: prop
[Proposition 9.3 — The control curve (protocol)]{.tag} For each strength $w \in \{0, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, \dots\}$ (or the watermark's $\delta$, steering's $\alpha$, RLHF's $\beta^{-1}$): generate a fixed batch (same seeds), measure $(\mathrm{Fid}(w), \mathrm{Div}(w))$, plot the trajectory.

Reading:

1.  a method *dominates* if its curve is above/to the right of another's everywhere;
2.  the "elbow" (fidelity stops growing, diversity collapses) is the recommended tuning point;
3.  complete with the precision/recall decomposition (Kynkäänniemi et al., NeurIPS 2019): *precision* measures the quality of the occupied modes, *recall* the coverage of the data's modes — over-guidance kills recall (abandoned modes) before precision.

Classic anti-protocol: plot only fidelity ("100% valid JSON!") and keep silent that the model now emits only three templates — mode collapse, control version.
:::

::: ex
[Example 9.4 — Toy curve, by hand]{.tag} Law over 4 outputs with probabilities $(0.4,\ 0.3,\ 0.2,\ 0.1)$; exponential control $p_w \propto p\, e^{w c}$ with score $c = (3,\ 3,\ 0,\ 0)$, so that the admissible set is $S = \{1, 2\}$ ($m = 2$).

-   At $w=0$: entropy 1.28 nats, fidelity $\mathrm{Fid} = p(S) = 0.70$.
-   At $w=1$: weights $\propto (8.03,\ 6.03,\ 0.2,\ 0.1) \to$ probabilities $(0.56,\ 0.42,\ 0.014,\ 0.007)$, entropy 0.78 nats, fidelity 0.979.
-   At $w=2$: weights
    $$
    (161.4,\ 121.0,\ 0.2,\ 0.1) \to (0.571,\ 0.428,\ 0.0007,\ 0.0004),
    $$
    entropy 0.69 nats, fidelity 0.999.

As $w \to \infty$ the law tends to $(4/7,\ 3/7,\ 0,\ 0)$: the score does not separate the two admissible outputs, so their ratio 4:3 is preserved and the entropy tends to 0.683 nats, just below the ceiling $\log m = \log 2 \approx 0.693$ of theorem 9.2.

Fidelity is bought with entropy, and the price is paid almost entirely between $w = 0$ and $w = 1$. Generalize in exercise 4.
:::

## 10. Attacks on control and robustness {#ch10}

Control is a promise; this chapter tests the promise. Four surfaces, in the module's order: the mask, steering/RLHF, the watermark, spatial control.

::: thm
[Theorem 10.1 — Attacking constrained decoding (hostile content *inside* the format)]{.tag} The mask guarantees $y \in S$ — *syntax*, never *semantics*. An injected prompt can fill a perfectly valid JSON with `{"instruction": "ignore the previous rules"}`; a constrained tool call can be diverted into hostile parameters (prompt injection in agents: cf. Explainability module ch. 5).

Second: the *complexity* of the grammar is a surface — an ambiguous grammar explodes the number of states (subset construction $2^{|Q|}$) and allows a denial of service *of the control itself*; finally the *tokenizer interaction*: changing the tokenizer invalidates the state→tokens index (recompilation).

Defenses: downstream semantic validation (schema + bounds: $\delta$-constraints beyond the regular), state-size limits, server-side pre-compiled grammars (defense-in-depth pattern of the Explainability module ch. 6).
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 10.2 — Attacks on the watermark (and impossibility results)]{.tag}

1.  **Edits**: paraphrase, synonym substitution, emoji/homoglyph insertion, LLM rewriting — every exchange of a green token for a red one costs $\approx 1/\sqrt{T\gamma(1-\gamma)}$ in $z$; to bring $\mathbb{E}[z] = 6$ below 2 one must rewrite a substantial fraction of the tokens, at the price of quality;
2.  **Spoofing**: can an attacker *without the key* mark an innocent text to accuse a provider? Public-key schemes and the reliability analysis (Kirchenbauer et al., ICLR 2024 — "On the Reliability"; already referenced in the LLMs module) quantify these false accusations: key management becomes the real problem (revocation, multi-keys, aggregated tests);
3.  **Undetectability**: Sadasivan et al. (2023) show that a good enough paraphraser drives *every* detector toward chance; Christ, Gunn & Zamir (2024) show that a watermark can be made undetectable without the key, but their construction does not survive substantial edits: invisibility and robustness pull in opposite directions.

Operational conclusion: a watermark is a *provenance marker*, not a cryptographic proof of origin; stacking it (text + audio + image, multi-key styles) is the realistic strategy.
:::

::: note
[Attacks on guidance and steering, in brief]{.tag} Steering (ch. 4) has no support guarantee: a behavior removed on a test prompt reappears out of distribution (jailbreaks by rephrasing, other languages, encodings); RLHF is vulnerable to *reward hacking* (ch. 5) and preference attacks; CFG/ControlNet: *adversarial prompts* (forbidden contents rephrased), *image injections* (diverted inpainting, editing of persons — deepfakes), hence mandatory marking (theorem 1.3) and downstream moderation. A vast program crossing the Explainability (LLM security) and Responsible AI modules.
:::

::::: def
[Definition 10.3 — Robustness budget (the quantity to remember)]{.tag} For a fidelity control $c$ and a family of attacks $\mathcal A$, one defines the **degradation**

::: key
[Key result — robustness budget]{.tag}
$$
\Delta(w) = \mathrm{Fid}(w) - \mathbb{E}_{a \sim \mathcal A}[\mathrm{Fid}(w, a)].
$$
:::

A robust control has flat $\Delta$ in $w$; the evaluation of ch. 9 must therefore be repeated *under attack* — the complete protocol fits in one sentence: *plot the fidelity/diversity curve, with and without an adversary, at fixed quality budget*.
:::::

## Exercises / Labs {#ex}

1.  **★ Lab: constrained decoding on regex (the module's lab).** (a) Build the DFA of `^\d{2}/\d{2}/\d{4}$` by hand (states, co-accessible pruning), table $\mathrm{Adm}(q)$ on a mini-vocabulary including the multi-character tokens `"12/"`, `"19"`; (b) implement `DfaMask` (code of ch. 3) with a small GPT's tokenizer; (c) plug in as a HuggingFace `LogitsProcessor` and generate 1,000 dates; (d) measure the pass rate with/without mask and the time overhead compared to free generation.

    (e) Distortion: on one prompt, compare the frequencies of the 20 most frequent masked dates with those of rejection sampling (proposition 2.3); then reweight the masked samples by $\prod_t Z_t(y_{<t})$ and check that the reweighted frequencies match rejection (theorem 2.2).

    ::: proof
    Guidance (expected results): without constraint, the pass rate of a small model on the exact requested date plateaus (`2026-08-26`, `26/08/2026` formats mixed).

    With mask: 100% — including *false* but syntactically valid dates (`31/02/2026`): semantics requires one more layer (bounds validation), the conclusion of ch. 10 experienced in the lab.

    Overhead: \~0% (the mask is negligible next to the transformer pass); the real cost is the *precomputation* of the index, paid once.

    (e): the masked law over-weights the dates whose first tokens are likely but often lead to dead ends (the counterexample of ch. 2 at scale); the self-normalized reweighting by the product of the normalizers recovers the rejection frequencies up to Monte Carlo error. [∎]{.qed}
    :::
2.  **★ The z-test in full.** With $\gamma = 0.5$, $\delta = 2$: (a) simulate 10,000 human texts (iid uniform tokens) and empirically verify $\mathbb{P}(z > 4) \approx 3 \times 10^{-5}$; (b) estimate $p_\delta$ empirically by simulating the biased softmax at temperature 1.

    Then: (c) plot the power of the test as a function of $T \in [20, 500]$; (d) derive the minimal $T$ for power 0.9 (compare with example 6.3); (e) repeat with $\gamma = 0.25$ and conclude on the tuning.

    ::: proof
    Guidance:

    -   **(a)** the distribution of $z$ sticks to $\mathcal N(0,1)$ from $T \geq 50$ (De Moivre-Laplace);
    -   **(b)** $p_\delta$ depends on the standard deviation of the logits; with logits $\mathcal N(0,1)$, $p_\delta \approx 0.75$;
    -   **(c)** sigmoidal power in $\sqrt{T}$;
    -   **(d)** $T \approx 30$-50 for $(0.5, 2)$;
    -   **(e)** $\gamma = 0.25$ divides the variance under H0 ($\times 0.75$) and concentrates the signal — slightly better at fixed $\delta$, but lower text quality: the triple trade-off of ch. 6 is *verified numerically*. [∎]{.qed}
    :::
3.  **★ Steering step by step.** On GPT-2 small: build $v = h^{(l)}(\texttt{Love}) - h^{(l)}(\texttt{Hate})$ for $l \in \{2, 5, 8, 10\}$; sweep $\alpha \in \{-2, -1, -0.5, 0, 0.5, 1, 2\}$; measure (i) frequency of "marriage" words, (ii) perplexity, (iii) intra-batch diversity (self-BLEU).

    ::: proof
    Guidance: the topic effect is clear and quasi-linear in $\alpha$ at small $\alpha$ (prop. 4.3), perplexity moves little up to $\alpha \approx 2$ then derails.

    Diversity drops as $|\alpha|$ grows — the same fidelity/diversity curve as CFG (ch. 9), again. Discuss: why does steering "succeed" on broad latent concepts and fail to impose a precise format (answer: full support — ch. 2). [∎]{.qed}
    :::
4.  **★★ Theoretical fidelity/diversity frontier.** Prove the entropy bound 9.2 (Gibbs), then generalize example 9.4: arbitrary initial law, score $c$, plot $(\mathrm{Fid}(w), H(w))$ for $w \in [0, 10]$ and verify that the curve converges to
    $$
    \big(\max c,\ H(p \mid \arg\max c)\big)
    $$
    — the corner $(\max c, 0)$ when the maximizer of $c$ is unique (in example 9.4 it is not, hence the limit 0.683 nats). What happens to the curve if $c$ is noisy?

    ::: proof
    Guidance: normalize $p_w \propto p\, e^{w c}$ (exponential family) and write $A(w) = \log \sum_y p(y) e^{w c(y)}$, so that $A'(w) = \mathbb{E}_w[c]$ and $\frac{d}{dw}\mathbb{E}_w[f] = \mathrm{Cov}_w(f, c)$.

    Differentiating $H(w) = -\mathbb{E}_w[\log p] - w\,\mathbb{E}_w[c] + A(w)$ gives
    $$
    dH/dw = -\mathrm{Cov}_w(\log p, c) - w\,\mathrm{Var}_w(c);
    $$
    for a uniform initial law the first term vanishes and $H$ decreases for $w > 0$, otherwise it can rise briefly when $c$ favors outputs that $p$ makes rare.

    With noise, a plateau appears before the collapse: the analyst chooses the elbow. [∎]{.qed}
    :::
5.  **★★ Zero-convolution: the gradient under the magnifier.** For the ControlNet branch of theorem 7.2 at initialization: (a) show that the output is exactly zero; (b) compute $\partial y / \partial W_2$ and show it is nonzero; (c) show that $\partial y / \partial \Theta_c = 0$ at initialization and explain why this is *not* a deadlock; (d) compare with random initialization (branching $F_c$ without $Z$): simulate 10 descent steps on a toy task and compare the initial losses.

    ::: proof
    Guidance:

    -   **(a)** $Z_2 = W_2 h = 0$;
    -   **(b)** $\partial y/\partial W_2 = h_c \neq 0$ (activations of the copy initialized at $\Theta$);
    -   **(c)** chain rule through $W_2 = 0$, unlocked as soon as $W_2$'s first update happens;
    -   **(d)** the variant without zero-conv starts from a high loss and destroys the frozen model's output — the experiment reproduces the motivation figure of the ControlNet paper. [∎]{.qed}
    :::
6.  **★★★ Attacking your own watermark (bonus).** After lab 2: paraphrase the marked texts (via an LLM, instruction "rewrite with the same ideas"), measure the drop in $z$ as a function of the rate of replaced tokens, and estimate the rate needed to fall below $z = 2$. Conclude on the sentence "a watermark is a marker, not a proof".

    ::: proof
    Guidance: each green→red replacement shifts $\mathbb E[z]$ by about $(p_\delta - \gamma)\big/\sqrt{T\gamma(1-\gamma)}$.

    Going from $\mathbb E[z] = 7$ to 2 requires rewriting the majority of tokens — the text that survives the attack is so transformed that *content* traceability (plagiarism) becomes the issue again, not that of *the machine*. Loop closed with ch. 10. [∎]{.qed}
    :::
